flawed_step: The first substantive step—claiming that connectivity and 3-regularity make the bridgeless hypothesis unnecessary—is false. A bridge can be forced into every perfect matching, and several such bridges can be incident to one vertex.
counterexample: Let the vertices be v and, for each i=1,2,3, five vertices x_i,a_i,b_i,c_i,d_i. Add edges vx_i and, within each i-th lobe, x_i a_i, x_i b_i, a_i c_i, a_i d_i, b_i c_i, b_i d_i, c_i d_i. This is a finite simple connected graph. Every vertex has degree 3: v is adjacent to x_1,x_2,x_3; each x_i is adjacent to v,a_i,b_i; and each of a_i,b_i,c_i,d_i has degree 3 from the listed lobe edges. Each vx_i is a bridge whose removal separates the five-vertex set {x_i,a_i,b_i,c_i,d_i}. Any perfect matching must contain vx_i, since otherwise those five vertices would have to be perfectly matched using only internal edges, which is impossible for an odd number of vertices. Thus a perfect matching would have to contain all three edges vx_1,vx_2,vx_3, but a matching cannot contain more than one edge incident to v. Hence this connected 3-regular graph has no perfect matching.
assessment_summary: The claim fails on an explicit 16-vertex connected simple cubic graph consisting of a central vertex joined by three bridges to three five-vertex cubic lobes. All three bridges are forced in any perfect matching, creating an impossibility at the central vertex.
